summary: Codex grades **modularity weak, reusability adequate, analysability weak, modifiability adequate, testability adequate** under ISO/IEC 25010. The workspace is an acyclic 133-crate DAG with a TUI that cannot bypass the API, yet change impact is wide: `codex-core` depends on 61 crates, and the `codex-protocol` vocabulary crate - 68 dependents, trapped by its own dependency on the network proxy and policy engine - is one side of the four strongest cross-component co-change pairs (metric:temporal_coupling). Analysability suffers from size rather than logic: 38 percent of main LOC sits in files over 1000 lines, the engine's config, session and event-translation files are each 3-4k lines, module docs are rare outside the TUI, user docs are off-site redirects, and v1/v2 generations compile side by side. Modifiability is helped by low unit complexity (2 percent of unit LOC in high-McCabe units) and a 117-flag, nine-layer configuration surface, and hurt by three engine merge magnets (`config/mod.rs`: 515 commits, 81 contributors) and 33 percent single-owner files. Testability rests on seams at the right boundaries and an integration suite that runs the engine for real; the sandbox and the vocabulary crate are the thin spots, and testing-scan's skip-macro and retry caveats apply. The **core engine costs the most** maintenance effort; the trajectory is improving slowly through a visible extraction programme. Sokrates supplied no component dependencies for Rust and caps its unit, duplicate and co-change exports at 10000, so those drivers carry lowered confidence. 14 findings: five verdicts and a posture (info), one medium trapped-crate and one medium hotspot-cluster finding, four low.

findings.title: Modularity: weak - a DAG with a god crate on top and a vocabulary crate that ripples into every layer
findings.description: System grade **weak**. Sokrates extracted no component dependencies for this Rust workspace, so fan-in/fan-out and cycles come from architecture-scan's manifest graph rather than from `metric:` data; confidence is lowered accordingly. Driver 1: the manifest graph is acyclic in production builds, but `codex-core` depends on 61 of 133 crates and is depended on by 23, so the compile-time seam around the engine constrains almost nothing and most changes rebuild the whole engine. Driver 2: change impact travels through the protocol crate rather than through imports - 4389 of the 10000 co-change pairs Sokrates kept cross component boundaries (metric:temporal_coupling), and the four strongest cross-component pairs all have `codex-rs/protocol/src/protocol.rs` on one side (141 shared commits with the TUI, 110 with app-server, 100 with the MCP server, 90 with core). Driver 3: the ext/* extension seam holds in one direction only - the traits are clean but ten of twelve extensions still link `core`. What keeps this off `poor`: the TUI genuinely does not link `core`, and no production cycle exists. Component grades sit in `attributes.components`: the protocol crate is `poor` because every field added there reaches 68 dependents at once; `auth`, `code-mode`, `sdk` and `repo tooling` are `strong` leaves with one or zero co-change partners.

findings.title: Cross-component co-change runs through protocol.rs - and the top pair is partly history, not the current shape
findings.description: Sokrates' temporal coupling shows the protocol crate as the hub of shotgun surgery: `protocol.rs` co-changed 141 times with `tui/src/chatwidget.rs`, 110 with `app-server/src/bespoke_event_handling.rs`, 100 with `mcp-server/src/codex_tool_runner.rs` and 90 with `core/src/session/mod.rs` (metric:temporal_coupling). The script's scenario ranking is built on these raw counts, which are un-normalised and span the whole 491-day history. Reading tempers the top pair: since the March 2026 rewrite the TUI consumes `app-server-protocol` notifications and `chatwidget.rs` contains a single `EventMsg` reference, so the 141 shared commits mostly predate the current architecture; the live ripple for an `EventMsg` change today is `protocol.rs` -> `bespoke_event_handling.rs` -> the v2 `ServerNotification` enum -> the TUI's `app_server_events.rs`, plus `codex_tool_runner.rs` in the deprecated MCP server. That is still four components for one enum variant. The pattern risk-synthesis explains for `EnvironmentConfig` (protocol data, core semantics, 100 percent co-change) is the same mechanism one level down.

findings.title: Reusability: adequate - 24 real leaf utility crates, but the vocabulary crate everyone reuses drags the proxy and policy engine with it
findings.description: System grade **adequate**. Driver 1 (positive): the workspace is deliberately split into small crates, and most of them are libraries in fact - 17 of the 24 `codex-rs/utils/*` crates depend on no other workspace crate or only on sibling utils, and `codex-protocol`, `app-server-protocol`, `apply-patch`, `execpolicy` and the SDKs each have more than one consumer. Driver 2 (negative): the most reused asset is trapped - `codex-protocol` (68 dependents) depends on `codex-network-proxy`, `codex-execpolicy` and `codex-http-client`, so nobody can reuse the vocabulary without compiling a TLS proxy; details in `reusability/trapped-protocol`. Driver 3: reuse by copy is small in volume - 302 of the 10000 duplicate blocks Sokrates kept span components, 12.9 percent duplication overall (metric:duplication) - but the pairs that exist are the hand-written parsers and fixtures a shared crate should own (`reusability/copy-instead-of-reuse`). Two further utilities point back at the product: `utils/oss` links `codex-core` and `utils/plugins` links `codex-exec-server`, which makes them engine adapters wearing a utils path. Component grades: `protocol` and `core` are `weak` (trapped or unreusable by design), `persistence`, `exec-server`, `model backends`, `configuration`, `auth`, `code-mode` and `sdk` are `strong` as crates with a manifest, a narrow API and external consumers.

findings.title: codex-protocol is the workspace's most reused asset and it cannot be reused without the proxy and the policy engine
findings.description: `codex-protocol` is the serde vocabulary 68 of 133 crates depend on and the one crate an external integrator would want on its own. Its manifest makes that impossible: it pulls `codex-network-proxy` (an HTTP and SOCKS5 proxy with a TLS stack), `codex-execpolicy` (the Starlark rule engine) and `codex-http-client`. architecture-scan documents the inversion; the maintainability cost is that the vocabulary crate has the **poorest modularity grade** in the workspace (every field added reaches every layer, and its four strongest co-change partners sit in four different components) while being the thinnest-tested one (testing-scan: ratio 0.08 path-based). The fix is mechanical and bounded - move `RequirementsExecPolicy`, `EnvironmentNetworkPolicy` and the `HttpError` wrapper behind a small trait or into a `protocol-policy` crate - which is why this earns `medium` rather than `low`.

evidence.note: the vocabulary crate links the proxy implementation

findings.recommendation: Cut the three service-crate edges out of `codex-protocol`: keep the policy and network vocabulary as plain data types here and move the evaluation logic and the `HttpError` conversion into the crates that own them. Add a CI check that `codex-protocol` depends only on `utils/*` and serde-level crates.

Between `protocol/src/permissions.rs` and `windows-sandbox-rs/src/resolved_permissions.rs` the script counts 586 duplicated lines in 29-line blocks of `FileSystemSandboxEntry` construction, the reuse-by-copy signal between the vocabulary and the sandbox backend. Volume is low for the workspace (302 cross-component blocks), so this is a `low` finding with two concrete targets rather than a systemic one.

findings.title: Analysability: weak - the code is well named and the contributor guide is real, but the files a newcomer needs are huge, module docs are rare in the engine, and user docs live off-site
findings.description: System grade **weak**. Driver 1: size - 38 percent of main LOC sits in files over 1000 lines and 61 percent in files over 500 (metric:unit_size, script from files.json); the three files a typical change needs, `core/src/config/mod.rs` (3837 LOC), `protocol/src/protocol.rs` (3057) and `app-server/src/bespoke_event_handling.rs` (3937), are each a day's reading. Sokrates inflates this somewhat because it counts inline `#[cfg(test)]` modules (140k LOC per testing-scan) as main code, but the three files above are production code. Driver 2: documentation - the top-level `docs/` pages are three-line redirects by policy, the one substantive protocol document describes the v1 model that domain-language-scan shows is a generation behind, and the doc footprint of 32k lines (45 doc lines per kLOC, script) is mostly `README.md` per crate plus the 322-line `AGENTS.md`, which is the genuinely useful map. A grep of `//!` crate and module docs across the 2130 main Rust files (a reading count, not a Sokrates metric) finds them in 63 percent of TUI files but 9 percent of core and 7 percent of app-server files. Driver 3: naming and generations - `session` carries three meanings, `Conversation*` aliases survive as `#[deprecated]` re-exports in `core/src/lib.rs`, and v1 and v2 API modules, `compact_remote` and `compact_remote_v2`, `guardian` and `guardian-v2` all compile side by side, so a reader cannot tell the live path from the legacy one without git. What keeps this off `poor`: names inside the code are precise, hotspot units read as rule-per-branch logic (risk-synthesis), and `AGENTS.md` states the layering rules in plain words. Component grades: `core` is `poor` (largest files, fewest module docs, most legacy aliases), `sdk` is `strong`.

findings.title: Modifiability: adequate - low logical complexity and a strong configuration surface, offset by three merge-magnet files and 33 percent single-owner files
findings.description: System grade **adequate**. Driver 1 (positive): logical complexity is low - only 2 percent of unit LOC sits in high or very-high McCabe units (script, on Sokrates' capped 10000-unit export), and risk-synthesis found the flagged units to be rule-per-branch validators rather than tangled logic. Driver 2 (positive): behaviour is configured, not hardcoded - a 117-entry feature-flag registry, a nine-layer config stack and generic `-c key=value` overrides mean many product changes are a flag flip (`modifiability/configurability`). Driver 3 (negative): change concentrates in a few central files that everyone edits - `core/src/config/mod.rs` with 81 contributors and 515 commits, `core/src/tools/spec_plan.rs`, `app-server/src/request_processors/thread_processor.rs` with 43 contributors (metric:commits, metric:contributors); `modifiability/hotspot-cluster-core-engine` covers the cluster. Driver 4: ownership - 33 percent of main files have a single contributor (metric:contributor_share, script), rising to 57 percent in persistence and 66 percent in code-mode, though project-level bus factor is healthy and the named single-owner areas are peripheral. Driver 5: duplication at 12.9 percent (metric:duplication) is mostly within components (302 of 10000 blocks cross them). Fix-vs-feature share is 18 percent fix, 25 percent feature, 5 percent refactor over all 9546 first lines (script keyword classification, 53 percent unclassified because 2026 titles use bare imperatives) - the script cannot split this per component, so the fix-heavy-areas driver is a data gap; evolution-scan reads the same messages as fixes falling from 23 to 12 percent. Component grades: `core`, `app-server` and `protocol` are `weak` (the merge magnets and the ripple source), the rest `adequate`, `sdk` `strong`.

findings.title: The core engine's config, tool-registry and session files are where every feature lands - and where 46 percent of recent commits go
findings.description: Three files in `codex-rs/core` form one cluster that every feature touches: `config/mod.rs` (3837 LOC, 515 commits, 57 in 90 days, 81 contributors), `tools/spec_plan.rs` (1289 LOC, 121 commits, 42 in 90 days) and `session/mod.rs` (2715 LOC, 384 commits) (metric:commits, metric:commits_90d, metric:contributors). risk-synthesis explains each file; the maintainability point is the shape: a new feature adds a resolver to config, a gated `registry.add` to spec_plan, and a branch in the session loop, so three of the four largest engine files change together for unrelated reasons, and 81 people merging into one file is a standing conflict cost. The core component also carries the highest commit count of any component (10544 file-commits, script) and, per evolution-scan, 46 percent of recent commits despite the extraction programme; the repo's own `AGENTS.md` says to resist adding code here. `core` is graded `weak` on modularity, analysability and modifiability and is the most-changed area, but `strong` on testability (ratio 2.16, the wiremock integration suite), which is why this is `medium` rather than `high`: changes here are expensive and collide, but they are caught.

findings.title: Configurability: most behaviour is a flag, a config layer or a `-c` override away - the strongest modifiability asset
findings.description: Codex avoids a large class of code changes by configuration. The `FEATURES` registry in `codex-features` holds 117 entries with a stage each, any of which a user flips with `--enable`, `codex features enable` or `features.<key>` in config; `config.toml` is resolved through nine precedence layers plus `requirements.toml` for managed pins; and every frontend accepts generic `-c key=value` overrides through `codex-utils-cli`, so a new setting does not need a new flag. The cost side is real but belongs to analysability: with 41 flags under development and both v1 and v2 paths compiled, the set of behaviours a build can exhibit is far larger than the set it ships, and `spec_plan.rs` gates tools on three different vocabularies (risk-synthesis). Neutral fact; no action.

findings.title: Testability: adequate - the design's seams sit at process and provider boundaries, and the parts behind them are tested for real; the sandbox and the vocabulary are the exceptions
findings.description: System grade **adequate**. Driver 1 (positive): the design's seams are where the architecture puts its boundaries - `ExecBackend` in exec-server, `TimeProvider` and `AttestationProvider` in core, `AuthProvider` in codex-api, the JSON-RPC process boundaries - and testing-scan shows the engine is exercised through them with only the model faked (`wiremock` at `/v1/responses`), giving core a 2.16 test ratio and app-server 1.23. Driver 2 (negative): the same boundaries that make the engine testable make its lower layers hard to test in isolation: the sandboxing and policy component sits at 0.26 and its OS-level tests are platform-gated and self-skipping, and the protocol crate at 0.08 path-based is guarded only by serde round-trips, so a renamed variant is caught downstream by snapshots (both `weak`). Driver 3: global state is modest for 97k LOC of engine - 31 `static`/`OnceLock`/`LazyLock` sites in core, mostly caches and templates - but one is a test-mode global (`testability/global-state`), and 54 env mutations in tests need `serial_test`. Driver 4, rolled up by reference: 1320 `skip_if_*` macro sites report pass when they skip and nextest retries every test once, so a green run proves less than it appears to (testing-scan). Component grades follow testing-scan's ratios where the design does not contradict them: `core`, `app-server`, `extensibility`, `exec-server`, `auth`, `code-mode`, `sdk` are `strong`; `protocol`, `sandboxing`, `repo tooling` are `weak`.

findings.title: Global state in the engine: a test-mode switch baked into ThreadManager and process-wide caches
findings.description: Global mutable state is limited but two shapes work against isolation. `thread_manager.rs` carries `FORCE_TEST_THREAD_MANAGER_BEHAVIOR`, a process-wide `AtomicBool` that changes production code paths when tests set it - a test hook inside the object under test rather than an injected collaborator, and one that leaks between tests in the same binary. `connectors.rs` keeps `ACCESSIBLE_CONNECTORS_CACHE` as a `LazyLock<Mutex<Option<..>>>`, so connector availability is memoised per process and tests that need a different answer must reset or serialise. These are the patterns behind the 54 environment mutations and 25 `serial_test` files testing-scan counts; the engine's other statics are message templates and model presets. `low`: contained, named, and the integration harness already works around them.

evidence.note: test behaviour switched by a process-wide global
process-wide cache with no injection point

findings.recommendation: Replace the `FORCE_TEST_*` global with a constructor parameter or a `ThreadManager` builder option, and give the connectors cache an owner (the session or thread manager) so tests get a fresh one per instance.

findings.title: Maintainability posture: modularity weak, reusability adequate, analysability weak, modifiability adequate, testability adequate; the core engine costs the most; trajectory improving slowly
findings.description: **Modularity weak**: no production cycles and a TUI that cannot bypass the API, but a 61-crate-fan-out engine and a vocabulary crate whose changes ripple into four components. **Reusability adequate**: dozens of real leaf crates, one trapped crate (`protocol`) and a handful of copied parsers. **Analysability weak**: precise names and a good `AGENTS.md`, but 38 percent of main LOC in files over 1000 lines, few module docs in the engine, off-site user docs and two generations of API compiled side by side. **Modifiability adequate**: complexity is low and behaviour is configurable, but three engine files are merge magnets with 40-80 contributors each and a third of files have one owner. **Testability adequate**: seams at the right boundaries and an integration suite that runs the engine for real, with the sandbox and the vocabulary thin and a green run that can hide skips. The **costliest component is the core engine**: weak or poor on four of five sub-characteristics, 46 percent of recent commits, and the place the repo's own guidance says not to grow. **Trajectory: improving slowly** - evolution-scan shows a deliberate extraction programme (config, models, http-client, ext/* crates), a flat high-velocity plateau with a broadening team, and fix-share falling; the counter-signal is that core's share of activity has not dropped. Highest-leverage changes: cut the service-crate edges out of `codex-protocol` (`reusability/trapped-protocol`), break up the core config and tool-registry cluster along the extension seam (`modifiability/hotspot-cluster-core-engine`), and generate the v2 notification projection instead of hand-mirroring `EventMsg` (`modularity/cross-component-cochange`). Data gaps: Sokrates extracted no component dependencies for this Rust workspace, its unit, duplicate and co-change exports are capped at 10000 entries, and the commit-mix could not be split per component.

evidence.snippet: Over time, the `codex-core` crate (defined in `codex-rs/core/`) has become bloated because it is the largest crate, so it is often easier to add something new to `codex-core` rather than refactor out the library code you need so your new code neither takes a dependency on, nor contributes to the size of, `codex-core`.
evidence.note: the repo's own statement of where maintenance effort concentrates
